questions.stem: Review the nurse's note. Highlight the findings that require immediate follow-up.

segments.text: 88/52 mm Hg, down from a baseline of 142/84

rationale.correct: Acute confusion, hypotension, tachycardia and a high lactate show sepsis with organ hypoperfusion.

perOption.s2: Acute confusion in an older adult can be the first sign of sepsis and poor brain perfusion.
perOption.s4: A risk factor for urinary tract infection, but not an acute finding.
perOption.s6: A large drop from baseline suggests septic shock.
perOption.s8: Tachycardia is a compensatory response to infection and low blood pressure.
perOption.s10: A lactate above 2 mmol/L shows tissue hypoperfusion.
perOption.s12: Acceptable for now; continue to monitor.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize the cues of sepsis in an older adult.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence based on the client's data.

content.template: The client's findings are most consistent with {{b1}} caused by {{b2}}.

options.text: hypovolemic shock from poor intake alone

rationale.correct: An older adult with UTI symptoms, fever, hypotension and a high lactate has urosepsis with shock.

perOption.b1:a: Infection with hypotension and a lactate above 2 mmol/L meets the picture of septic shock.
perOption.b1:b: Poor intake contributes, but fever, leukocytosis and a positive urinalysis point to sepsis.
perOption.b1:c: A glucose of 264 mg/dL is far below the levels seen in HHS.
perOption.b2:a: Dysuria and a urinalysis with nitrites and leukocyte esterase identify the source.
perOption.b2:b: Breath sounds and oxygenation don't point to a lung source.
perOption.b2:c: Confusion is explained by sepsis, and there are no focal deficits.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
NCSBN NCLEX-RN Test Plan
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Analyze cues to identify urosepsis.

questions.stem: For each complication, indicate whether the client is at high or low immediate risk based on the current data.

rationale.correct: Shock threatens the kidneys and other organs, and delirium raises injury risk.

perOption.r1:c1: Creatinine has nearly doubled from baseline with hypotension.
perOption.r1:c2: Rising creatinine shows the kidneys are already affected.
perOption.r2:c1: Blood pressure is still falling and lactate is high.
perOption.r2:c2: Falling blood pressure shows shock is progressing.
perOption.r3:c1: Nothing in the data suggests eye disease.
perOption.r4:c1: Acute confusion in an older adult raises fall risk.
perOption.r4:c2: Delirium is a strong fall risk factor.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Prioritize the most likely complications of septic shock.

questions.stem: Which prescriptions should the nurse anticipate for this client? Select all that apply.

options.text: Two sets of blood cultures before antibiotics
Encourage 240 mL of oral fluids every hour
Hold the insulin until the blood pressure is normal

rationale.correct: Hour-1 sepsis bundle: lactate, cultures, antibiotics, fluids, then vasopressors if hypotension persists.

perOption.a: Cultures identify the organism and should be drawn before the first dose.
perOption.b: Early antibiotics lower deaths from sepsis.
perOption.c: Recommended for hypotension or a lactate of 4 mmol/L or more; this client is hypotensive.
perOption.d: A falling lactate shows that perfusion is improving.
perOption.e: Oral intake cannot correct septic shock in a confused client.
perOption.f: Glucose still needs management; hyperglycemia worsens outcomes.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
NCSBN NCLEX-RN Test Plan
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Plan sepsis bundle care.

questions.stem: Place the nurse's actions in the order they should be done.

items.text: Draw two sets of blood cultures
Give the first dose of IV antibiotic

rationale.correct: Access, cultures, fluids and antibiotics come first; monitoring follows.

perOption.a: Access is needed for fluids and medications.
perOption.d: Antibiotics are started within the first hour, after cultures.
perOption.e: Urine output shows whether kidney perfusion is improving.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Sequence nursing actions in septic shock.

questions.stem: Four hours later the nurse reassesses the client. For each finding, indicate whether it shows improvement or no improvement.

rows.text: Oriented to person, place and time

rationale.correct: Blood pressure, lactate and mental status have improved; low urine output still needs follow-up.

perOption.r3:c2: The kidneys are still poorly perfused; report it.
perOption.r4:c1: Mental status has returned to baseline.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Evaluate the response to sepsis treatment.

questions.stem: Select the 4 findings that show the child's asthma exacerbation is severe.

rationale.correct: Severity signs: limited speech, retractions, hypoxemia and low peak flow.

perOption.b: Accessory muscle use shows increased work of breathing.
perOption.c: Hypoxemia below 90% marks a severe exacerbation.
perOption.e: A low-grade temperature isn't a severity sign.
perOption.f: The cold is the likely trigger, not a sign of severity.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize a severe pediatric asthma exacerbation.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence.

content.template: The child's wheezing and hypoxemia are caused by {{b1}}, most likely triggered by {{b2}}.

rationale.correct: A viral infection triggered airway inflammation and bronchospasm.

perOption.b1:a: Asthma narrows and inflames the lower airways.
perOption.b1:b: That describes pneumonia or pulmonary edema.
perOption.b1:c: Upper airway obstruction causes inspiratory stridor, not expiratory wheezes.
perOption.b2:a: Viral colds are the most common trigger of asthma flares in children.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Analyze the cause of an asthma exacerbation.

questions.stem: The child is frightened and clinging to the parent, has had little to drink since the afternoon and used the inhaler without a spacer at home. Which problem is the nurse's priority for this child?

options.text: Impaired gas exchange from narrowed airways
Anxiety that is making the breathing worse
Risk for dehydration from rapid breathing
Ineffective inhaler technique without a spacer

rationale.correct: Oxygenation comes first.

perOption.a: An SpO2 of 89% from narrowed airways is the most immediate threat.
perOption.b: Fear adds to the distress but is secondary to the hypoxemia.
perOption.c: Possible with tachypnea and poor intake, but not the most urgent.
perOption.d: This likely contributed, but teaching comes after the child is stable.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Prioritize gas exchange in acute asthma.

questions.stem: For each category, select the actions the nurse should anticipate in the emergency department.

options.text: Repeat respiratory assessment after each treatment

rationale.correct: Acute asthma care: oxygen, short-acting bronchodilators with ipratropium, systemic steroids and close monitoring.

perOption.a: A short-acting beta2 agonist relieves bronchospasm quickly.
perOption.b: Added to albuterol in severe exacerbations to improve bronchodilation.
perOption.c: Reduces airway inflammation; the effect begins within hours.
perOption.d: Cough suppressants and opioids can depress breathing and aren't used.
perOption.g: Not useful in the acute phase.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Plan acute asthma treatment for a child.

questions.stem: The provider has prescribed oxygen, nebulized albuterol with ipratropium, oral dexamethasone and a chest x-ray. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Apply oxygen and start the albuterol-ipratropium nebulizer
Give the oral dexamethasone so it can start working sooner
Send the child for the chest x-ray before treatments begin
Weigh the child to confirm the doses of each medicine

rationale.correct: Treat breathing first.

perOption.a: This treats the hypoxemia and bronchospasm right away.
perOption.b: Steroids take hours to work; oxygen and bronchodilators act in minutes.
perOption.c: Imaging does not treat the problem and should not delay treatment.
perOption.d: A recent or estimated weight can be used; treatment should not wait.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Take action in an acute pediatric asthma exacerbation.

questions.stem: One hour after treatment, the nurse reassesses the child. For each finding, indicate whether it shows improvement or decline.

rationale.correct: Drowsiness during an asthma attack is a danger sign, not a sign of rest.

perOption.r3:c2: Drowsiness may signal CO2 retention and impending respiratory failure.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)

questions.stem: Highlight the findings that are severe features of preeclampsia.

cells: Headache unrelieved by acetaminophen with visual spots

rationale.correct: Severe features include BP of 160/110 or more, platelets under 100,000, raised liver enzymes, and neurologic or visual symptoms.

perOption.r1: 160/110 mm Hg or higher on two readings is a severe feature.
perOption.r3: New neurologic and visual symptoms are severe features.
perOption.r4: Edema is common in pregnancy and isn't a diagnostic criterion.
perOption.r5: Liver enzymes at least twice the upper limit of normal are a severe feature.
perOption.r6: A reassuring fetal heart rate pattern.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize severe features of preeclampsia.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence.

content.template: The client is at highest immediate risk for {{b1}}, as shown by {{b2}}.

options.text: headache, visual changes and hyperreflexia with clonus

rationale.correct: Persistent headache, visual changes and clonus warn of impending eclampsia.

perOption.b1:a: Cerebral irritability in severe preeclampsia can progress to seizures.
perOption.b1:b: A later risk, not the most immediate one.
perOption.b2:a: These are warning signs of impending eclampsia.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Analyze seizure risk in severe preeclampsia.

questions.stem: The client is anxious, the face and hands are swollen, the fetal heart rate is reassuring and the platelets are 96,000/mm3. Which problem is the nurse's priority?

options.text: Risk for seizures and stroke from severe hypertension
Risk for bleeding related to the low platelet count
Risk for fetal compromise from reduced placental flow
Fluid volume excess shown by the facial edema

rationale.correct: Preventing eclampsia and stroke comes first.

perOption.a: Eclampsia and stroke are the most immediate threats to the client's life.
perOption.b: Platelets above 50,000 rarely bleed on their own; seizures and stroke are more imminent.
perOption.c: The fetal heart rate is reassuring; the maternal threat is more immediate.
perOption.d: Edema is common in pregnancy and secondary here.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Prioritize problems in severe preeclampsia.

questions.stem: For each intervention, indicate the goal or goals it supports. Each row may have more than one answer.

rationale.correct: Severe preeclampsia: magnesium for seizure prevention, rapid antihypertensives, fetal monitoring and a low-stimulation environment.

perOption.r1:c1: Magnesium is the drug of choice to prevent eclamptic seizures.
perOption.r1:c2: Magnesium isn't used as an antihypertensive.
perOption.r3:c3: It shows how the fetus tolerates the maternal condition and treatment.
perOption.r4:c2: It doesn't directly lower blood pressure.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Plan care for severe preeclampsia.

questions.stem: Magnesium sulfate is started. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Check respiratory rate and deep tendon reflexes every hour
Keep calcium gluconate at the bedside
Use an infusion pump on a secondary line
Encourage the client to walk to the bathroom
Stop the infusion when the headache goes away

rationale.correct: Magnesium sulfate safety: pump, hourly reflexes, breathing and urine output checks, and calcium gluconate ready.

perOption.a: Loss of reflexes and slow breathing are early signs of toxicity.
perOption.b: Magnesium is excreted by the kidneys; low output raises the risk of toxicity.
perOption.c: Calcium gluconate is the antidote for magnesium toxicity.
perOption.e: Seizure and fall risk require bed rest with the side rails padded.
perOption.f: Magnesium usually continues for 24 hours after birth.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Take action safely during magnesium sulfate therapy.

questions.stem: Two hours later, the nurse reassesses. For each finding, indicate whether the treatment is effective or not effective.

rationale.correct: Controlled BP, no seizures and normal reflexes show success; a respiratory rate under 12 signals toxicity.

perOption.r2:c1: The goal of magnesium therapy is met.
perOption.r3:c1: A slow rate isn't a treatment goal.
perOption.r3:c2: Suggests magnesium toxicity; stop the infusion and notify the provider.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Evaluate preeclampsia treatment.

questions.stem: Select the 4 findings that most suggest alcohol withdrawal.

rationale.correct: Withdrawal signs: tremor, sweating, tachycardia, hypertension, agitation, hallucinations and seizures.

perOption.a: Tremor is one of the earliest signs of withdrawal.
perOption.b: Visual hallucinations occur 12 to 48 hours after the last drink.
perOption.c: Autonomic hyperactivity raises the heart rate.
perOption.e: This explains the timing (no access to alcohol), not a sign itself.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize alcohol withdrawal after surgery.

questions.stem: For each time after the last drink, select the withdrawal finding most typical of that period.

rationale.correct: The client's day-2 picture (hallucinations, fever, autonomic signs) fits progression toward delirium tremens.

perOption.b1:b: DTs typically begin at 48 to 72 hours.
perOption.b2:a: Alcoholic hallucinosis and withdrawal seizures peak in this window.
perOption.b2:c: Wernicke's is from thiamine deficiency, not a stage of withdrawal.
perOption.b3:a: DTs: confusion, severe autonomic instability and fever.
perOption.b3:b: By this time severe withdrawal may develop.
perOption.b3:c: This is when the most dangerous phase can begin.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Analyze the timeline of alcohol withdrawal.

questions.stem: The client keeps trying to stand on the operated ankle, has a temperature of 38.0 °C and pulled at the IV once overnight. Which problem is the nurse's priority?

options.text: Risk for injury from withdrawal seizures and delirium
Risk for infection shown by the new low-grade fever
Risk for falls from standing on the operated ankle
Ineffective denial of the client's alcohol use

rationale.correct: Safety from seizures and delirium comes first.

perOption.a: Withdrawal can progress to seizures and delirium tremens, which can be fatal.
perOption.b: Fever here fits autonomic hyperactivity of withdrawal; infection is assessed but is less urgent.
perOption.c: Falls are part of the injury risk, but seizures and DTs are the larger threat.
perOption.d: This is addressed after the client is safe.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Prioritize safety in alcohol withdrawal.

questions.stem: Which interventions should the nurse anticipate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Benzodiazepine dosed by a withdrawal scale such as CIWA-Ar
A dark, quiet room with the door closed

rationale.correct: Withdrawal care: benzodiazepines, thiamine, fluids and electrolytes, safety and low stimulation.

perOption.d: Darkness creates shadows the client may misperceive; a quiet, well-lit room is better.
perOption.e: Restraints are a last resort and can increase agitation.
perOption.f: Clients in withdrawal often need fluids and electrolytes.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Plan alcohol withdrawal care.

questions.stem: The client's CIWA-Ar score is 22. The client last had lorazepam 2 mg 1 hour ago and is still agitated. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Give the lorazepam dose the protocol lists for this score
Wait until the 4-hour reassessment before giving another dose
Give haloperidol for the agitation instead of lorazepam
Apply wrist restraints until the agitation settles

rationale.correct: Symptom-triggered benzodiazepine dosing based on CIWA-Ar score.

perOption.a: A score above about 15 to 20 indicates severe withdrawal; symptom-triggered dosing can repeat hourly.
perOption.b: Delay risks seizures and delirium tremens.
perOption.c: Antipsychotics do not treat withdrawal and lower the seizure threshold.
perOption.d: Restraints are a last resort and can increase agitation.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Act on a withdrawal assessment score.

questions.stem: Six hours later, for each finding, indicate whether it shows improvement or no improvement.

rationale.correct: Falling heart rate and fewer symptoms show improvement; a seizure is a serious complication.

perOption.r4:c2: Shows progression; needs urgent treatment and safety measures.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)

caseStudies.title: Older adult with sepsis from a urinary tract infection

exhibits.title: Emergency department, 14:00
exhibits.body: A 78-year-old client is brought in by their daughter, who says the client has been "more confused since yesterday" and has eaten little. History: type 2 diabetes, hypertension, benign prostatic hyperplasia. The client is oriented to person only. Skin is warm and flushed; mucous membranes are dry. The client reports burning on urination for 3 days.

rows.label: Urinalysis
cells: Positive leukocyte esterase and nitrites, many bacteria

caseStudies.title: Child with a severe asthma exacerbation

exhibits.title: Pediatric emergency department, 19:20
exhibits.body: A 7-year-old with asthma has had a cold for 2 days. Tonight the child is coughing and wheezing; the parent gave albuterol twice at home with little relief. The child is sitting upright, speaking in short phrases, with intercostal and subcostal retractions. Expiratory wheezes in all lung fields.

caseStudies.title: Preeclampsia with severe features at 35 weeks

exhibits.title: Labor and delivery triage, 10:10
exhibits.body: A 24-year-old client, gravida 1, at 35 weeks reports a headache for 6 hours that acetaminophen didn't relieve and "seeing spots." Swelling of the face and hands. Fetal heart rate 145/min with moderate variability.

exhibits.title: Orthopedic unit, postoperative day 2, 06:00
exhibits.body: A 52-year-old client had open reduction and internal fixation of the ankle 2 days ago. Overnight the client became restless and sweaty, with a tremor of both hands. At 05:45 the client said, "There are bugs crawling on the wall." The client's spouse says the client drinks about a pint of vodka a day; this wasn't documented on admission.
